text: This is Quiet Hours. A household admin autopilot, built with the Strands Agents SDK and running on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. It does the routine work in the background, and only interrupts you when there is a real decision to make.

Here's the problem. Running a home is a stream of small, boring, slightly risky tasks. The water bill. The electricity bill that is suddenly double. The dentist recall, the permission slip due Friday, the delivery that needs a signature when nobody is home. And the urgent overdue invoice that is actually phishing. None of it is hard. All of it costs attention, usually in the evening, when attention is scarcest.

It's for busy parents, and anyone who runs a household. Most assistants are one more app to open. Quiet Hours is the opposite. Every action passes a deterministic autonomy policy before it runs. Anything the policy won't sign off becomes a single decision card, with the reason. And every answer is remembered, so it interrupts you less each week.
Let's watch it work. This is the Rivera household in Austin, on a fresh day. I'll advance the simulated clock, and a day of mail arrives: seven items, shown as tiles.

Now a background sweep. Normally EventBridge Scheduler triggers this every thirty minutes. A fast model triages every item, then one specialist agent per item reads the household profile, the bill history and the calendar, and picks a tool. Before any tool that spends money or signs something runs, the autonomy policy decides: proceed, or pause and ask.

Three things were handled quietly. The water bill was paid, because it's a recurring vendor within twenty five percent of its usual amount. The dentist was booked on a Tuesday at three thirty, which is the family's preferred window. The UPS delivery was moved to Saturday morning. And the phishing invoice was flagged and blocked. It will never be paid.

Three things need a human. Look at the electricity bill: two hundred fourteen dollars, eighty one percent above the usual. The card says exactly why it's asking. Under the hood this is a Strands interrupt: the agent is frozen mid tool call, its session parked in S3. I'll approve it, and trust this vendor from now on.

The tap resumed the same session in a new AgentCore invocation, and the payment ran with the exact arguments that were frozen. The insurance renewal is up eighteen percent, so I'll decline that one and shop around. And I'll approve the field trip form, which needed my signature and a twelve dollar fee. Notice the standing permission that just appeared: pay Austin Energy, up to about two hundred forty six dollars. That's also written to AgentCore Memory.

Day two. The internet bill and the pediatrician were handled on their own. Two asks: a new piano teacher's invoice, because the vendor has never been paid before, and a Netflix price increase. I'll trust the piano teacher, and decline the price increase.

Day three. Four things handled quietly, and only one ask. The piano invoice was paid without asking this time, because I trusted that vendor yesterday. The corrected electricity bill was back in its normal range, so it just went through.

This is the point of the product. Interruptions went from three, to two, to one, while the quiet work went up. The agent gets quieter the longer it runs, and every action carries the reason it was allowed.
You can also just ask it. Why did you pay the piano invoice without asking me? It answers from its own audit log.

The architecture. A Strands agent on AgentCore Runtime, with a triage agent, per item specialists, thirteen household tools, and the Human In The Loop intervention driven by a policy classifier. Interrupts park in S3 and resume later. AgentCore Memory learns preferences. EventBridge Scheduler calls a Lambda, which invokes the runtime. DynamoDB holds items, actions and decision cards. Slack gets one card per real decision, with signed one tap links. And a Next.js dashboard on Vercel is the live demo.
Quiet Hours. Fewer pings every week, and every action explained. The code is open source, and the demo is live. Thanks for watching.
